def format_summary(result: dict[str, object]) -> str:
    """Plain-text summary for the terminal.

    Parameters
    ----------
    result : dict
        ``VideoResult.model_dump(mode="json")``.

    Returns
    -------
    str
        Scores in context and the notes.
    """
    video = result["video"]
    assert isinstance(video, dict)
    lines = [
        f"{video['name']}  {video['duration_s']:.1f} s  {video['width']}x{video['height']}  {video['n_clips']} clips",
        "",
    ]
    reading = result.get("reading")
    if isinstance(reading, dict):
        lines += [str(reading["headline"]), *reading["reasons"], str(reading["action"]), ""]
    models = result["models"]
    assert isinstance(models, dict)
    for score in models.values():
        ctx = score["context"]
        label, odds = rarity(ctx["real_rank"], score["name"])
        low, high = (round(v * 100) for v in ctx["real_range"])
        lines.append(
            f"{score['name']:<7} probability of fake {round(score['fake'] * 100)}%  "
            f"[{score['device']} {score['precision']}]",
        )
        lines.append(f"        {label}: {odds} (real videos usually {low}–{high}%)")
        if score.get("device_note"):
            lines.append(f"        note: {score['device_note']}")
    lines.append("")
    notes = result["notes"]
    assert isinstance(notes, list)
    for note in notes:
        prefix = {"at_risk": "!", "breaks": "!", "partly": "~", "holds": "-", "info": " "}[note["state"]]
        lines.append(f"{prefix} {note['text']}")
    lines += ["", "Scores are model outputs and can be wrong. Use --json for every value and detail."]
    return "\n".join(lines)

docs.title: FAQ
docs.text: Common questions about what MARScope does and does not do. For the details, see How it works; for setup, see Installation.

docs.title: Does MARScope tell me whether a video is fake?
docs.text: No. It shows what three detectors output, how unusual each score is for that model, what each model relies on, and how far to trust it. It never says a video is real or fake, and it sets no threshold on a score. There are three reasons: the scores are uncalibrated, the models often disagree, and a single answer is easily mistaken for evidence.

docs.title: Why does MARScope still leave the decision to me when every model gives a high score?
docs.text: Agreement makes a reading more consistent, but the three models were trained on the same videos and can share blind spots. And when fakes are rare, even a detector that is right most of the time is often wrong about the videos it flags. The Learn tab shows this with numbers.

docs.title: What does "very unusual for a real video" mean?
docs.text: Among the real videos the model was tested on (11,098 of them), very few scored this high: "fewer than 1 in 100 real videos score this high on MARS". Each model has its own usual range, so the same score can be normal for one model and unusual for another, which is why models are compared this way and never by raw score. It describes the score; what the video shows is for you to judge.

docs.title: Why does a model show 100%?
docs.text: That is the score the model gave, shown as it is. A model can be fully confident and still be wrong; the assumption tests show whether that confidence survives simple changes to the video.

docs.title: Why do the models disagree?
docs.text: They read different things: MARS looks at the whole frame over time, while GenD and DFD-HR score frames one by one. Videos unlike the training data are where detectors drift apart. When they disagree, the next step is to check where the video comes from.

docs.title: Which videos work best?
docs.text: Videos like the training data: face videos (FF++) and rendered footage (GTA-V), at least one full clip long (about 4 seconds), not heavily compressed. On videos with no face, from a new generator, very short or heavily compressed, scores are less reliable, and the notes say so (assumption A3).

docs.title: Does my video leave my machine?
docs.text: No. The video and its frames stay on the machine that runs MARScope, and a job is deleted an hour after last use, or when you leave the result. The only outside calls are the model downloads from Hugging Face and, if you set one up, a language model.

docs.title: What does the language model receive?
docs.text: Only the structured result in words, the notes without their numbers and a plain description of your tests: never the video or frames. The report sheet shows exactly what was sent. Without a language model everything still works; the summary then comes from a template.

docs.title: Do I need a GPU?
docs.text: No, but it helps. With an NVIDIA GPU (Linux or Windows) a 10-second clip takes a few minutes with all three models; on the CPU it takes much longer. Apple silicon Macs run on the CPU.

docs.title: I see "Failed to load libcublasLt.so.12" and the model runs on the CPU
docs.text: The CUDA libraries are missing. Run uv sync --extra cuda, then start again with uv run --extra cuda marscope .... See Installation.

docs.title: How do I open the app from my laptop when it runs on a cluster?
docs.text: Start it with --host 0.0.0.0 and forward a port over SSH; see Web UI and serving.

docs.title: Can I use it on Google Colab?
docs.text: Not tested yet.

docs.title: Can I use the results as evidence, or to make a decision about a person?
docs.text: No. MARScope is an educational tool. Legal, forensic, journalistic and employment decisions, and claims about a person, need qualified experts and other evidence. Policy notes are general information, without legal advice (EU AI Act, Annex III 6(c)).

docs.title: Does it check audio or images?
docs.text: No, video frames only.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text: MARScope is a pipeline around three ONNX detectors. The detectors are unchanged research checkpoints; what MARScope adds is everything around the score: the frames are prepared exactly as in training, the score is placed among the model's test videos, the model is tested, and fixed rules explain the result. This page walks through what happens between choosing a video and reading the report.

docs.title: The pipeline at a glance
docs.text:
Video

MP4, MOV or WebM. Checked first: faces, bitrate, length and Content Credentials.

→

Clips

Every second frame, in 64-frame clips, prepared exactly as in training.

→

Models

MARS, GenD and DFD-HR score each clip (ONNX Runtime, GPU or CPU).

→

Context and tests

Each score placed among the model's test videos; A1, A4 and A5 re-score the strongest clips.

→

Notes and report

Fixed, cited notes from deterministic rules; a report with optional LLM prose.

docs.title: Frames and clips
docs.text:
The models only give meaningful scores on input prepared the way they were trained, so this part never changes:

  • Frames are decoded as RGB with PyAV, and every second frame is kept.
  • Kept frames are grouped in clips of 64. A short last clip is padded by repeating its last frame, and only its real frames count.
  • Each frame is resized to a square (bicubic, no crop) and scaled to [-1, 1].
  • A clip score is the model's probability of fake for that clip. The video score is the mean over clips.

Clip length, frame stride and image size are read from each model's ONNX metadata, not written in the code. On a GPU the models run in fp16 (the same results as the paper); on the CPU, in fp32.

docs.title: Scores in context
docs.text:
A raw score means little: one model may give most real videos 10% and another 50%. So each model comes with its usual ranges: the scores it gave the benchmark test videos (11,098 real, 12,435 fake), stored as 101 percentiles for each precision.

  • "Very unusual for a real video: fewer than 1 in 100 real videos score this high" says where the score sits among the model's real test videos, in plain odds. The app draws it as a bar: the band is where real videos usually score (from the lowest 5% to the highest 5%), the dot is this video.
  • A high fake score is one above the model's usual range for real videos (its 95th percentile). It describes the score; nothing is decided by it.
  • Models are compared by that place, never by raw score. The result says whether the models agree, and how consistent the evidence is (consistent, mixed or weak).

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
• MARS has built-in evidence: how much each frame and each area (a 24 × 24 grid) adds to its score. The app draws it on the frame and on the timeline.
  • GenD and DFD-HR have no built-in map. An occlusion map hides each area of an 8 × 8 grid in turn and measures how the score changes.
  • Tests against chance. "Hide its top frames" (or areas) removes what the model ranks highest and compares with removing as many at random. If the top picks move the score much more than random ones, the model relies on them.

Evidence describes what a model relies on, never where a forgery is.

docs.title: The assumptions, A1 to A5
docs.text:
Every detector rests on assumptions about what gives a fake away. MARScope asks five of them as questions, answered per model with measured numbers:

Question How it is answered A1 Does it break when the face outline (the seam of a face swap) is hidden? The face outline is blanked in the strongest clips, which are scored again. Needs a face A2 Does it break on a new generator? The model's results on generators it never saw (GenVideo, DF26) A3 Does it hold on videos unlike its training data? The checks before the models: faces, bitrate, length, shape A4 Does it break when the video is shared many times? The strongest clips at 40% resolution, light blur and noise, JPEG quality 35 A5 Does it break when fine pixel detail is removed? The strongest clips with their fine detail removed

The answer is judged against the model's own usual range for real videos:

  • Holds: the score stays where it was.
  • Partly: it falls, but stays higher than the model usually gives real videos.
  • Breaks: it falls into the model's usual range for real videos, so the model needed what the test removed.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
Deterministic rules turn the measured values into notes, in English or French:

  • How far to trust the models: A1–A5, per model.
  • Where the video comes from: whether the file carries Content Credentials (C2PA), and what they say. Missing credentials prove nothing either way.
  • Laws and risks that may apply: labelling rules in the EU, intimate-image laws in Canada and the US, and the deepfake risks listed in the MIT AI Risk Repository.

Rules never change a score, give the same notes for the same video and versions, and attach their own references. Settings are provisional until they are checked on the test sets.

docs.title: The report
docs.text: The report is filled from a template: every number, note and reference comes from the result. A language model can write the connecting summary (optional, see Reports and Ask). It receives the result in words, the notes without numbers and a plain description of your tests, never the video or frames. Sentences with a number or a conclusion about the video, and references the rules did not attach, are removed; if anything fails, the template summary is used and the report says so.

docs.title: Ask
docs.text: General questions are answered from a small set of reviewed knowledge cards, written from our survey, the MARS paper and the MOZAIC benchmark, and found with a plain keyword search (no model, no network). Questions about a result go to the language model, if one is set up, with the result's facts and the closest cards; the same filter as the report applies. A question asking whether the video is real or fake always gets the fixed answer that leaves the decision to you.

docs.title: Privacy
docs.text: The video and its frames stay on the machine that runs MARScope. A job and its files are deleted an hour after last use, or when you leave the result. The only outside calls are the model downloads from Hugging Face and, if you set one up, the language model.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text: MARScope runs trained video deepfake detectors on a video and helps you read what they say. Each score is placed next to the scores the same model gives real and fake test videos, the evidence behind it is shown, and you can test what the model relies on. Fixed rules then write notes on how far to trust the result, with references. The decision about the video stays with you.

docs.title: A worked example
docs.text:
A 12-second face-swap clip from the Celeb-DF v2 test set, with all three models:

Model Probability of fake Compared with real videos MARS 66% Very unusual: fewer than 1 in 100 real videos score this high GenD 89% Very unusual: fewer than 1 in 100 real videos score this high DFD-HR 100% Very unusual: fewer than 1 in 100 real videos score this high

"66%" on its own says little: MARS gives most real test videos between 7% and 24%, so 66% is far above its usual range, while for GenD the same 66% would be normal. That is why every score comes with its place among the model's test videos, and why models are compared by that place, never by raw score.

The assumption tests then ask, for each model, whether the score breaks when something is removed:

Test MARS GenD DFD-HR A1: face outline hidden Holds Holds Holds A4: shared many times Breaks Breaks Breaks A5: fine pixel detail removed Holds Partly Holds

All three scores fall into the range the models give real videos when the clip is compressed and resized as if shared many times. A widely shared copy of this clip could pass all three detectors. That is the kind of thing MARScope is built to show.

docs.title: What you can do with a result
docs.text:
• Read the scores in context

    Each model's probability of fake, how unusual it is for a real video, and how the models agree or disagree.

  • See the evidence

    MARS's built-in maps of the frames and areas it relies on; occlusion maps for GenD and DFD-HR.

  • Test it

    Hide a model's top frames or areas and compare with hiding as many at random. The common test is computed in the background, so it is usually ready the moment you press it.

  • Ask "what if"

    Change JPEG quality, resolution, blur and noise, or simulate a copy shared many times, and see every score move.

  • Read the notes

    How far to trust the models (A1–A5), where the video comes from (Content Credentials), and laws and risks that may apply in the EU, Canada and the US.

  • Keep a record

    A report with what you tried (Markdown, HTML, PDF), an evidence card (PNG) and a session file. Ask questions about the result.

docs.title: Who it is for
docs.text: Anyone who wants to understand video deepfake detection rather than trust a single number: people running workshops and courses, journalists and fact-checkers learning how detectors behave, researchers comparing detectors, and policy teams who need to know what these tools can and cannot do.

docs.title: What it does not do
docs.text:
• The decision stays with you. MARScope reports what each detector measured, with no threshold on a score.
  • For learning. Scores are model outputs and can be wrong. Legal, forensic, journalistic and employment decisions, and claims about a person, need qualified experts and other evidence.
  • Video only. No audio, no images.
  • Not everything. The models were trained on face videos (FF++) and rendered game footage (GTA-V). On videos unlike that, scores are less reliable, and the notes say so.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
Install MARScope from the repository and analyze your first video. The models (about 0.8 GB each) download from Hugging Face the first time they are used.

Web UI (GPU)Web UI (Mac or CPU)Command linePython 
git clone https://github.com/VectorInstitute/marscope.git
cd marscope
uv sync --extra cuda
uv run --extra cuda marscope --serve
# open http://localhost:8000/app

git clone https://github.com/VectorInstitute/marscope.git
cd marscope
uv sync
uv run marscope --serve
# open http://localhost:8000/app

uv run --extra cuda marscope --video clip.mp4                        # MARS
uv run --extra cuda marscope --video clip.mp4 --models all --report pdf

from marscope import MARScope
from marscope.analysis.ranges import rarity

scope = MARScope(models="mars,gend")
result = scope.analyze("clip.mp4")
for model in result.models.values():
    print(model.name, f"probability of fake {model.fake:.0%}", rarity(model.context.real_rank, model.name))

In the app: choose a video (up to 2 minutes and 1080p), and press Analyze. MARS runs by default; tick GenD and DFD-HR under Choose models to compare. By default you are asked to guess real or fake before any score is shown.

On a remote GPU machine or a cluster, see Web UI and serving. For platforms and GPU setup, see Installation.

docs.title: Command line
docs.text:
Analyze a video and print the scores in context:

uv run --extra cuda marscope --video clip.mp4

Choose the models, print every value as JSON, or write a report next to the video:

uv run --extra cuda marscope --video clip.mp4 --models mars,gend      # MARS alone is the default
uv run --extra cuda marscope --video clip.mp4 --models all
uv run --extra cuda marscope --video clip.mp4 --json
uv run --extra cuda marscope --video clip.mp4 --report pdf          # writes clip-report.pdf
uv run --extra cuda marscope --video clip.mp4 --language fr --jurisdiction eu

Start the web UI and REST API instead (see Web UI and serving):

uv run --extra cuda marscope --serve

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option What it does --video PATH / --serve Analyze one file, or start the web UI and REST API --models mars (default), gend, dfd-hr, comma-separated, or all --sequential One model at a time, for a small GPU --device auto (default), cuda or cpu --precision Model file on the GPU: auto (fp16, default) or fp32. The CPU always runs fp32 --no-faces Skip face detection (A1 and the face checks of A3 are then skipped) --json Print the full result as JSON --report markdown, html or pdf, written next to the video --no-llm Use the template summary even if a language model is set up --language en (default) or fr, for notes and reports --jurisdiction eu, ca, us or all: which laws the context notes mention --host, --port Where --serve listens (default 127.0.0.1:8000) --verbose Log each step

docs.title: Exit codes
docs.text:
Code Meaning 0 Done 2 The file is missing or cannot be read as a video, or an option is wrong (for example an unknown model)

An analysis of a 10-second clip with all three models takes about 2 to 3 minutes on one GPU, including loading the models; most of it is the assumption tests.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
MARScope is not on PyPI yet. Install it from the repository with uv:

git clone https://github.com/VectorInstitute/marscope.git
cd marscope
uv sync --extra cuda       # NVIDIA GPU on Linux or Windows
uv sync                    # Apple silicon Mac, or a machine without an NVIDIA GPU

Then run commands with uv run --extra cuda marscope ... (or uv run marscope ... without a GPU). Keeping --extra cuda on uv run means a later update of the lock file still installs the CUDA libraries.

Once MARScope is released: pip install marscope[cuda] (GPU) or pip install marscope.

docs.title: Where it runs
docs.text:
Machine Runs on Linux x86_64 or Windows x64 with an NVIDIA GPU (laptop, workstation, cluster node) GPU, fp16 Apple silicon Mac, ARM Linux, Windows on ARM CPU, fp32 Any machine without an NVIDIA GPU CPU, fp32
  • Python 3.12 to 3.14.
  • GPU memory: 2.3–2.9 GB per model in fp16, so all three fit on an 8 GB card. --sequential runs one model at a time.
  • CPU: works everywhere ONNX Runtime does, but much more slowly; the result says when a model ran on the CPU.
  • Intel Macs are not supported: ONNX Runtime no longer publishes wheels for them.
  • Google Colab is not tested yet.

docs.title: The cuda extra
docs.text:
ONNX Runtime's GPU build needs the CUDA 12 and cuDNN 9 libraries. The cuda extra installs them as Python wheels, so nothing has to be installed system-wide, and any NVIDIA driver from CUDA 12 on works (newer drivers too). On a machine that already has CUDA 12 and cuDNN 9 installed, plain uv sync is enough.

If CUDA cannot be loaded, the models fall back to the CPU and you see a warning such as:

Failed to load libcublasLt.so.12: libcublasLt.so.12: cannot open shared object file
WARNING MARS: CUDA could not be loaded (CUDA 12 or cuDNN 9 libraries missing), so the model runs on the CPU with the fp32 file

The fix is uv sync --extra cuda, then start again with uv run --extra cuda ....

docs.title: Check that the GPU is used
docs.text:
• The app's start screen shows "GB of GPU memory free" (or "No GPU found").
  • Every score shows where it ran, for example cuda fp16.
  • uv run --extra cuda marscope --video clip.mp4 --json has "device": "cuda" for each model.

docs.title: Where files go
docs.text: What Where Change it with Models The Hugging Face cache (~/.cache/huggingface) HF_HOME Face detector and other small files ~/.cache/marscope MARSCOPE_CACHE A job's video and frames (server) A temporary folder, deleted with the job

docs.title: Optional: a language model for the report
docs.text: See Reports and Ask.

docs.title: Python API
docs.text:
from marscope import MARScope
from marscope.analysis.ranges import rarity

scope = MARScope(models="mars,gend")      # device="auto", precision="auto", sequential=False, faces=True
result = scope.analyze("clip.mp4", jurisdiction="eu", language="en")

for model in result.models.values():
    print(model.name, f"probability of fake {model.fake:.0%}", rarity(model.context.real_rank, model.name))
    print("  ran on", model.device, model.precision)
    print("  clips:", [round(c.fake, 3) for c in model.clips])

print(result.agreement.strength)          # "consistent", "mixed" or "weak"
for note in result.notes:
    print(note.kind, note.state, note.title)

result is a Pydantic VideoResult; result.model_dump_json() gives the same JSON as --json. The models load once per MARScope and stay loaded, so reuse the object for several videos.

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Argument Values models "mars,gend", a list, "all", or None for MARS only (the default) device "auto", "cuda" or "cpu" precision "auto" (fp16 on the GPU, fp32 on the CPU), "fp16" or "fp32" sequential Run one model at a time, whatever the free GPU memory faces Detect faces (needed by A1 and the face checks of A3)

docs.title: Tests and reports
docs.text:
from marscope.explain.report import build_report, to_markdown, to_pdf
from marscope.explain.ask import chip_answer

scores = scope.rescore("clip.mp4", result, clip_index=0, drop=[2, 5])   # every model, two runs removed
curve = scope.sweep("clip.mp4", result, "mars", clip_index=0)           # top frames against random

report = build_report(result, use_llm=False, language="en")
print(to_markdown(report))
open("report.pdf", "wb").write(to_pdf(report))

print(chip_answer(result, "tests").text)                              # a fixed answer, no LLM

See the API Reference for every class and function.

docs.title: The report
docs.text:
In the app, Report opens the report sheet; on the command line, --report markdown|html|pdf writes it next to the video. It contains:

  • a short summary, and who wrote it (the template, or a named language model);
  • the scores in context, per model;
  • What you tried: the tests you ran in the app (frames hidden, top frames or areas against random, occlusion maps, What if edits), with the scores the toolkit measured;
  • the notes, the references they cite (and only those), the versions and the disclaimer.

Exports from the sheet:

Export What it is Copy The report as Markdown, on the clipboard Download PDF, HTML or Markdown, in the app's language Session (JSON) The full result, your tests, the report text and your guess Evidence card One PNG: the scores and their place, the trust results, the note on how to read them and the versions

Tick Include the current frame to put the frame you are on in the evidence card, the PDF and the HTML report. Nothing includes a frame unless you ask, and every file is saved on your machine.

docs.title: A language model for the summary (optional)
docs.text:
Without a language model, the summary is a fixed template. To have one write it, add any OpenAI-compatible endpoint to a .env file in the folder you run MARScope from (start from the repository's .env.example: cp .env.example .env):

MARSCOPE_LLM_BASE_URL=https://your-endpoint/v1
MARSCOPE_LLM_API_KEY=...
MARSCOPE_LLM_MODEL=model-name      # exactly as the endpoint lists it (names are case-sensitive)

What it receives and what is kept:

  • Sent: how unusual each score is for a real video (in words), the notes with their numbers removed, and your tests in words ("large drop", "little change"). Never the video or frames.
  • Kept: only sentences with no number (in digits or words) and no conclusion about the video, and only references the rules attached. Every number in the report comes from the template.
  • If it fails (no answer within 40 seconds, an error, or prose that breaks the rules), the template summary is used and the report says why.

The report sheet shows exactly what was sent, under Sent to the language model.

docs.title: Ask
docs.text:
The Learn tab has Ask about this result:

  • Suggested questions ("Why do the models disagree?", "What do the A1–A5 results say?", "What would make this more certain?", "So is it real or fake?") get fixed answers built from the result. They work without a language model and give the same answer every time.
  • General questions ("What is a deepfake?", "What is C2PA?", "What should our team do?") are answered from MARScope's knowledge cards: short answers written from the cited research papers (survey, MARS, MOZAIC) and reviewed. The card's own text is shown, with its references, so these answers work offline and never change.
  • Questions about this result go to the language model with the result's facts, the closest cards as background, and the same filter (at most three short sentences, no numbers, no conclusion about the video). Without a language model, they get a card only when one answers them closely.
  • A question asking whether the video is real or fake ("Is this fake?") always gets the fixed answer, which leaves that decision to you, and never reaches the language model.

docs.title: REST API
docs.text: marscope --serve exposes the API the web UI uses. Interactive docs are at http://localhost:8000/api/docs.

docs.title: Analyze a video
docs.text:
# upload: returns {"id": "...", "status": "queued"}
curl -s -F video=@clip.mp4 -F models=mars,gend http://localhost:8000/jobs

# progress as server-sent events, until "done"
curl -N http://localhost:8000/jobs/<id>/events

# the result
curl -s http://localhost:8000/jobs/<id>

# the report as PDF
curl -s -X POST -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"format": "pdf"}' \
     http://localhost:8000/jobs/<id>/report -o report.pdf

# delete the video and the result now
curl -s -X DELETE http://localhost:8000/jobs/<id>

docs.title: Endpoints
docs.text:
Endpoint What it does GET /health Status, GPU, free memory, whether a language model is set up GET /models · GET /benchmark · GET /references Models (memory, typical scores), benchmark results, the reference list POST /jobs Upload a video (form fields video, models, jurisdiction, language); returns a job id GET /jobs/{id}/events Progress (server-sent events): stages, clips, tests GET /jobs/{id} The result: scores, evidence, notes GET /jobs/{id}/frames/{n}.jpg · GET /jobs/{id}/maps/{model}/{clip} Frame thumbnails; MARS patch maps POST /jobs/{id}/rescore Score one clip again with some frames removed (every model) POST /jobs/{id}/sweep · POST /jobs/{id}/probe A model's top frames or areas removed, against random (computed once per job; record: false keeps a background run out of the report) POST /jobs/{id}/occlusion An 8 × 8 occlusion map for one clip POST /jobs/{id}/edit · POST /jobs/{id}/quality-sweep What if edits on one clip; the same at JPEG 100 to 10 POST /jobs/{id}/notes The notes again for another region or language (scores do not change) POST /jobs/{id}/report The report as JSON, Markdown, HTML or PDF (format, language, optional frame) POST /jobs/{id}/ask A suggested question (chip) or your own (question) DELETE /jobs/{id} Delete the video and the result now

Errors come back as {"error": "..."} with a 4xx status (for example 400 for a file that is not a video, 404 for an unknown job, 409 while a job is still running).

docs.title: Web UI and serving
docs.text:
uv run --extra cuda marscope --serve

Open http://localhost:8000/app (the landing page is at /). The same server exposes the REST API.

Option Default What it does --host 127.0.0.1 Interface to listen on. The default keeps the app reachable from this machine only --port 8000 Port --models mars Models loaded at start; the others load when picked on the start screen --precision auto fp16 on the GPU unless fp32 is asked for; the CPU always runs fp32 --device auto cuda or cpu to force one

docs.title: Using the app
docs.text:
1. Choose a video (MP4, MOV or WebM, up to 2 minutes and 1080p), pick the models, and press Analyze. With Guess first on, you guess real or fake before any score is shown.
  2. While it runs, one card per model fills in clip by clip, then each test lights up as it runs.
  3. The result: a frame viewer with the model's map, a timeline with every clip's score per model, and four tabs:
  4. Check: the evidence and the tests against chance. The common test is computed in the background while you look around, so pressing it usually answers at once; nothing is shown until you press it.
  5. Notes: how far to trust the models (A1–A5), provenance, and laws that may apply, by region.
  6. What if: JPEG quality, resolution, blur, noise, or "shared many times", and every score again.
  7. Learn: the five assumptions, the MIT AI Risk Repository, how far one score goes, the model cards, and Ask.
  8. Report: the report sheet, with Copy, Download (PDF, HTML, Markdown, session JSON) and the evidence card. See Reports and Ask.

The app is in English and French, with light and dark themes.

docs.title: On a remote GPU machine or a cluster
docs.text:
Run the server on the GPU machine and let it listen on its network interface:

uv run --extra cuda marscope --serve --host 0.0.0.0

Then, on your laptop, forward a local port to it, through the login node if there is one:

ssh -N -L 8010:<gpu-node>:8000 <user>@<login-host>

and open http://localhost:8010/app. After you log in, the command stays silent: the tunnel is open until you stop it.

  • <gpu-node> is the machine the server runs on (on Slurm, the node name squeue shows).
  • VS Code and Cursor can forward the port for you from the Ports tab instead.

\"Address already in use\"

Something on your laptop already holds that local port: often an older tunnel still running in another terminal, or your editor's own port forwarding. Pick another local port (-L 8020:...), or find what holds it with lsof -nP -iTCP -sTCP:LISTEN and close it.

Shared machines

With --host 0.0.0.0, other users of the network can reach the app. Jobs and their videos are deleted an hour after last use, or when you leave the result.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text: Uploads are checked before a job is created: the file type by its content, at most 500 MB, 2 minutes and 1080p. The server runs one analysis at a time per GPU and queues the rest.

docs.title: Development
docs.text:
Set up the environment with uv:

uv sync --extra cuda       # or plain `uv sync` without an NVIDIA GPU
source .venv/bin/activate
pre-commit install

Checks run before every PR (see CONTRIBUTING.md):

uv run pre-commit run --all-files               # ruff, ruff-format, mypy, typos, doctest, unit tests
uv run pytest -m "not integration_test" tests   # unit tests: no models, GPU or network
uv run mypy src
uv run mkdocs build --strict                    # when docs change

Integration tests (-m integration_test) load the real models and check that the pipeline reproduces the research outputs on fixed clips. They need a GPU and local copies of those clips (MARSCOPE_DATA_ROOT), so they run on a GPU machine, not in CI. Run them before merging any change to preprocessing, the model runners, score aggregation or the usual ranges. On a Slurm cluster, run them through the scheduler:

srun --partition=<gpu-partition> --gres=gpu:1 --cpus-per-task=8 --mem=32G --time=01:00:00 \
    uv run --extra cuda pytest -m integration_test tests

What reviewers check, and what blocks a merge, is in REVIEW.md.

docs.title: Build the docs locally
docs.text:
uv sync --group docs
uv run mkdocs serve

Then open http://127.0.0.1:8000. If that port is in use (for example by marscope --serve), run uv run mkdocs serve -a 127.0.0.1:8001.
